auxiliary_material: The text outlines the biological relevance of SCFAs in immune system development, glucose homeostasis, and inflammation, providing context for why these metabolites are monitored. It includes a troubleshooting guide for common GC-MS issues such as vacuum pressure leaks, column bleed, and poor analyte recovery. The authors note that SCFAs are highly hydrophilic and volatile, necessitating specific derivatization to improve detection sensitivity. The paper mentions that the method was validated for micro-scale biological samples and demonstrates excellent linearity (R2 ≥ 0.95) for calibration curves.
outline_action: Search for peer-reviewed methodological papers specifying LC-MS/MS or GC-MS parameters for inosine quantification in human biofluids or tissue. Identify protocols specifically validated for tumor tissue metabolite extraction and processing. Locate clinical studies or consensus guidelines that report absolute physiological concentrations of SCFAs in cancer patient cohorts to establish disease-specific reference ranges.
remaining_gap: The supplied material does not address quantification protocols for inosine, leaving that component of the gap question unanswered. The protocol is validated for human serum and feces, not tumor tissue, so the success criterion regarding tumor sample analysis remains unmet. While healthy control reference ranges are cited from an external database (HMDB), the study does not provide cancer-specific reference ranges or consensus statements for SCFA concentrations in oncology patients. The study explicitly states no new data were created or analyzed, meaning it does not establish empirical reference ranges from a cancer cohort.
useful_material: This study provides a detailed Basic Protocol for quantifying 14 short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in human serum using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). It specifies analytical platform parameters including the use of an Agilent 7820A GC-5977B MSD system, an HP-5 ms capillary column (30 m x 250 μm x 0.25 μm), oven temperature programming (60 °C to 325 °C), and electron impact ionization at -70 eV. The authors describe sample processing standards involving alkaline extraction (0.1 M NaOH for serum), methanol precipitation, vacuum concentration, and derivatization with N-tert-butyldimethylsilyl-N-methyltrifluoroacetamide (MTBSTFA) at 60 °C. The protocol includes storage recommendations (−80 °C for long-term) and cites the Human Metabolomics Database (HMDB) for normal concentration ranges of acetic acid in human blood (26.8 to 64.2 μM) as a reference for healthy controls.
